blocks.title: The Water Cycle
blocks.subtitle: How water moves continuously between the sky, land, and oceans.

blocks.text: Heat from the sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and rivers. Molecules at the surface gain enough energy to escape as water vapor. Plants also release vapor through transpiration.
As water vapor rises, it cools. Cooler air holds less vapor, so the vapor turns back into tiny liquid droplets that cluster together to form clouds.
When droplets grow heavy, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. The water then flows as runoff into rivers, soaks into the ground, or is stored as ice, completing the loop.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: The water cycle has no true start or end. The same water is recycled over and over.

blocks.title: Tracing one puddle
blocks.body: A puddle forms after morning rain. By midday the sun heats it and water evaporates (1). The vapor rises, cools, and condenses into a cloud (2). That cloud later drops rain on a hillside (3), and the water runs downhill into a river that reaches the sea, where evaporation begins the cycle again.
blocks.takeaway: Every drop is part of a loop, not a one-way trip.

questions.question: What process turns liquid water into water vapor?
questions.explanation: Evaporation is driven by heat energy, such as heat from the sun.

questions.question: Which process forms clouds?
questions.explanation: Water vapor cools and condenses into droplets, which gather to form clouds.

questions.question: What is the role of precipitation in the water cycle?
options: It returns water from clouds to land and water bodies
It removes salt from the oceans
It turns ice directly into water vapor
questions.explanation: Precipitation moves water from the atmosphere back to the surface, where it can collect and be recycled.
